extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers (Spectator readership): gentlemen, cultivated public interested in morals, rhetoric, translation, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and literary essays (The Spectator) offering prescriptive remarks on social behaviour, rhetoric, translation, education, and public policy. The texts mix observation, anecdote, and prescriptive advice aimed at improving manners, taste, and civic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ridicule to cure the extravagancies of love
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule, perhaps, is a better Expedient against Love than sober Advice. Hudibras and Don Quixote may be as effectual to cure the Extravagancies of this Passion, as any of the old Philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer satirical or comic exemplars to solemn philosophical counsel when attempting to check romantic folly. The author plans to publish (and cites) a 'Greek' manuscript and literary examples as cures; note that authenticity of such exempla should be treated with caution (anachronisms/orthography may indicate spuriousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling the inquisitive / talkative person
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquisitive are the Funnels of Conversation; they do not take in any thing for their own Use, but merely to pass it to another. They repeat almost verbatim what was said to them and are the Channels through which all the Good and Evil that is spoken in Town are conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not entrust secrets to inquisitive people; if offended by them you may 'mend that Inconvenience' by supplying them with corrective detail (they will propagate it). Expect them to accept and transmit idle particulars; use that tendency to your advantage to contradict or spread information as needed. Anti-pattern: giving them confidential matters which will quickly be disseminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity (without malice) as a source of humour and conversational material
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mind which is gratified this Way is adapted to Humour and Pleasantry, and formed for an unconcerned Character in the World; this Curiosity... lays up in the Imagination a Magazine of Circumstances which cannot but entertain when they are produced in Conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate non-malicious curiosity to accumulate entertaining particulars for conversation and writing. Such an imaginative store provides material for humour and a 'mere Spectator' stance. Use gathered details to enliven conversation rather than to harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating loud talkers (the Licinius instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caius Gracchus used a servant Licinius with a Pitch-pipe to regulate his voice; when a soft note was sounded C. would abate and grow calm. The author has had an instrument made and intends to furnish coffee-houses or private users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy for noisy or long-winded speakers: employ a soft audible signal (a 'Licinius' or pitch-pipe) to remind or check speakers. Distribute or place such instruments in public rooms; privately warn habitual offenders ('Get a Licinius'). Improvement: include a 'Hush-Note' specifically for long stories, swearing, obscenity, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for faithful lyric/poetic translation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation renders the original's short turns of expression, emotion, and 'spirit'; one should preserve the same elegance and vehemence of sentiment. The author compares Catullus, Boileau, and an English translation of Sappho to illustrate fidelity vs imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer translations that keep the original's brevity, turn of phrase, and passionate sequence of circumstances rather than loose imitations that supply poetry but not passion. Use critical authorities (e.g., Longinus) to judge whether a translation captures the 'spirit' and natural imitation of effects in the original. Anti-pattern: treating translation as mere poetic imitation which loses the specific emotional progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using medical/poetic symptoms as accurate depiction (diagnostic realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longinus has observed that Sappho's description of Love is an exact Copy of Nature: faltering voice, burning blush, languid eye, sudden sweat, tumultuous pulse, swoon and paleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing intense states (love, passion) in writing or diagnosis, assemble a sequence of realistic physiological and behavioral symptoms to give credibility and vividness. Rhetorical/useful as diagnostic signs (as in Plutarch's anecdote of Antiochus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate modesty in public speaking and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A just and reasonable Modesty is requisite to an Orator; Cicero liked an Orator who appeared in some little Confusion at the Beginning. Modest Merit has a double Claim to Acceptance; modesty heightens virtues and acts as a guard to vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a balanced modesty: slight nervousness or deference before an audience gains sympathy and patrons, whereas 'Meer Bashfulness without Merit is awkward' and 'Merit without Modesty, insolent'. Anti-patterns: excessive modesty that prevents performance, or vicious modesty that shuns serious or virtuous action or is shamefaced about circumstances beyond one's control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness versus modesty: beware of hollow civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Politeness among the unthinking treats Impudence as good Breeding, recommends shamelessness as being 'in Countenance', and thus undermines Morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage an outward politeness that excuses vice or promotes immodesty. True modesty and private self-scrutiny (Seneca's prescription: imagine Cato before you) are more effective moral checks than fashionable civility. Anti-pattern: socially-approved impudence and shamelessness masked as 'good breeding'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of youth by refined amusements and progressive classical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed scheme: retire a small number of youths to an agreeable solitude near a city to instruct them in music, dancing, drawing, design, and other accomplishments; cultivate taste in native language before Latin, read best Roman historians and poets, give short chronology/geography/medals/astronomy, exercise style in light native-language writing, recitations, and acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach taste and language by pleasant, social, accomplishment-based methods rather than drudgery: awaken relish for fine writing before imposing difficult classical languages; use recitation, acting, and shared readings to instill appreciation; progressively introduce Latin when taste and general reading are formed. Aim to cultivate imagination, virtue, and public spirit as well as linguistic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable relief should promote labour, not idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants ought not to encourage Beggars; the Alms they receive are the Wages of Idleness. No man should take relief until he has first purchased as much as possible of his own livelihood by the labour of his own hands; public taxation should only make up the deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design parish relief and charity to encourage productive labour: require some effort or purchase of means to livelihood before dispensing public relief. Treat unconditional alms as counter-productive to commerce and manufacturing (creates consumers unable to buy local products). Policy anti-pattern: free alms that institutionalize idleness and depress domestic consumption.
